outcomes.question: Before I put time into this: is it well regarded? Has it been criticised or superseded?
outcomes.text:
Yes, it's worth the time. The essay won the 2025 Berggruen Prize Essay Competition [spya-gp3g6s], and it has drawn replies. [Ethics in Review](https://www.ethicsinreview.com/on-anil-seths-the-mythology-of-conscious-ai-part-1/) answers it directly. [Armando Vieira](https://medium.com/@Lidinwise/why-the-mythology-of-conscious-ai-misses-the-deeper-point-437589461d45) agrees with its critique of current AI but says biological naturalism leaves the explanatory gap open. Seth also [mentions](https://hraness.com/reading/anil-seth-bbs-conscious-ai-biological-naturalism-thread) a journal collection of commentaries on his work. I found nothing saying it has been superseded.

Sources › Reception, below, collects these. Do you want to read for the group's debate or for the argument itself?

outcomes.question: What should I read before or alongside this to get the most out of it?
outcomes.text:
You don't need anything first. The essay is self-contained. Alongside it, Seth's longer academic version, [Conscious artificial intelligence and biological naturalism](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/conscious-artificial-intelligence-and-biological-naturalism/C9912A5BE9D806012E3C8B3AF612E39A), gives the full argument. For a counterview, try [Contra Anil Seth](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/kAHar2hrQbykF9Rt7/contra-anil-seth-on-ai-consciousness), which attacks the rainstorm analogy [spya-npjt4j].

Does your group lean sceptical or sympathetic to AI consciousness?

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
Seth is a credentialed consciousness scientist: he directs Sussex's Centre for Consciousness Science [spya-rg493b]. But he is arguing for his own position, and he admits it's a minority view [spya-qu7j89] and that he has no knock-down argument [spya-hj5y6s].

Published critics say his case [leans on dualist intuitions](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/abs/metaphysical-confusion-and-biological-naturalism/1E4A6A9504C0ED3C541F063277A9F1AB) or that [life-like properties aren't unique to living things](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/abs/defining-biological-naturalism/DB189E6DFBF4DA270B9A009C18A91DBA). Those would make good discussion material.

Which side of the debate does your group lean toward?

outcomes.question: Before I put time into this: is it well regarded? Has it been criticised or superseded?
outcomes.text:
It's contested, and partly updated by its author. Gwern wrote a [follow-up two years on](https://gwern.net/scaling-hypothesis-revisited), which the piece itself points to [spya-suzdvz]. Critics include a paper arguing the [strong version is hard to falsify](https://exa.ai/library/publication/wvyyyj4b3l1) and a [causal-confusion objection](https://www.greaterwrong.com/posts/FZL4ftXvcuKmmobmj/causal-confusion-as-an-argument-against-the-scaling). For a reading group, that makes it a good argument to test, not a settled one.

outcomes.question: What should I read before or alongside this to get the most out of it?
outcomes.text:
Gwern's own follow-up, ["Scaling Hypothesis Revisited"](https://gwern.net/scaling-hypothesis-revisited), is the best companion. It looks back two years later at how his claims held up. Before reading, skim Kaplan et al's scaling-laws paper, which the "How far will scaling go?" section leans on [spya-sctj6d]. Sutton's "Bitter Lesson" [spya-sfkxh8] also helps. The Sources mode lists links for all of these.

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
Gwern Branwen is an independent, pseudonymous writer, not a lab researcher ([Google Scholar profile](https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=yk1QMowAAAAJ)). [Dwarkesh Patel's interview](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/gwern-branwen) presents him as an early observer of scaling. He is credible on tracking the evidence, but this is an advocacy essay. His own admission of earlier doubt is at [spya-emqjaa]. The "Critiquing The Critics" section is the most one-sided part [spya-zyncdd]. Read it as an argument, and check the forecasts yourself.

outcomes.question: Who is the author, and how far should I trust them on this subject?
outcomes.text:
Gwern is an independent writer. His [own page](https://gwern.net/me) calls him a freelance researcher, and [OpenReview](https://openreview.net/profile?id=%7EGwern_Branwen1) lists no publications. So this is an informed advocate's essay, not peer-reviewed work. One [commentary](https://itdoeswhatnow.com/m/2020-05-28-gwern-publishes-the-scaling-hypothesis/) calls it a synthesis, and says DeepMind's later Chinchilla results complicated its scaling picture.

For a reading group, the sections worth testing are the confident forecasts and the attacks on critics [spya-zyncdd]. He also admits his own earlier doubts [spya-emqjaa].
